String:
Acre: An Amazon tributary splits the teams
in the far west of Brazil; its fords are the
only ways across, and holding them wins the
game. The rainforest is dense, so wood never
runs out. There is no gold: Brazil's
greatest rubber producer pays its coin in
rubber trees. Tapirs are the main food, and
the river's fish a second source.
<font=MapDescRule 4><u> </u></font>

Amazonia: The mighty Amazon splits the teams
deep in the rainforest and has no fords:
build a navy to control the river and the
map, but watch for enemy towers and cannon
on the shore. Each game draws two trade
routes (one per bank), one or none, and
trade routes and natives may be split
between the banks... or not.

Anatolia: Also known as Asia Minor, this
land has seen countless wars. Teams start at
opposite ends of a dry peninsula with cliffs
and sea on two sides; land and sea are rich,
and the trade route is shared evenly. Ally
with the knights of the Order of Christ for
powerful units, and escort your ships:
galleys patrol the coast and can damage
them.
<font=MapDescRule 4><u> </u></font>

Andes: A mountainous map where the teams
start dangerously close, on either side of a
trade route with three Trading Post sites
that runs straight down the middle or bends
in a V; with the straight route, a river
with one ford may guard each side. Four
Aymara villages stand on the far side of the
map: allying with all of them is powerful.

Appalachians: Teams start on either side of
one or two long ridges, crossed only at a
few gaps: a defensive map, where you guard
or wall the gaps and fight for the valleys.
Each game draws one or two trade routes, up
to two native nations and one of four skins.

barren land, where trees, plants and animals
are very scarce. You will have to rely on
trade to build an empire, so the posts along

Araucania: A long strip of South America's
west coast, between the Pacific and the
impassable cliffs of the Andes, with
plentiful hunting, fishing and whaling. Each
game draws one of three regions, the
northern desert rich in copper, the central
grasslands rich in food or the icy south
full of treasures, and one of three
coastlines.
<font=MapDescRule 4><u> </u></font>

Atacama: The driest non-polar desert in the
world: no natives live here, and guanacos
and trees are few. Salt mines are plentiful,
most of all in the middle, on the salt flats
(salares) where nothing can be built. Two
trade routes cross in the centre: hold them,
as they keep you fed when the rest runs out.

Lrg Cabos: Teams start on either side of a
long, arid peninsula, with a mountain range
and a trade route of three to five trading
sites down the centre. Two to five villages
of two native tribes vary each game. Fishing
is rich, with whales off the southern tip;
extra silver and gold are scarce, found
mostly in the mountains or the north.

the shore and give way first to mountains,
then to the Mojave Desert to the east. Two

on opposite sides of the map, and the trade
route always has four Trading Post sites.

shipment is ready quickly.

Manicouagan Basin: Resources are abundant in
the summer months of eastern Canada. Players
start around a ring of water that encloses a
large central island: compete for the land,
the water, the chokepoints and the native
allies at once. The Cree offer strong
technologies and an extra economic option,
the lake offers fish and a strategic edge,
but coin needs a strong presence on land.

Outback: This open land in northern
Australia is home to diverse flora and
fauna. The very large, open map leaves you
exposed to raids but rewards stealth and
expansion. A trade route to the south brings
extra income, with a river beyond it forded
at three shallows, and the Afghan cameleers
may prove powerful allies.

Western Territory: The rugged west of
Australia holds plenty of resources: gather
coin from valuable sandalwood in the dense
stands of trees, or mine it on the open salt
flats. Beware of raids in the open and in
the bush, as the cracked, arid ground makes
defences hard to build. The trade route
appears only with two teams.

the area, a great source of wealth. Holding
the map is nearly impossible with so much
open ground and steep hills.

Mapuche, an impassable cliff ringed by a
narrow river separates you from the enemy

beside a small trade route, absent in
free-for-all games.

Lrg Zavkhan: A winding river divides this
vast, remote region of Mongolia, forded at
three points (five with three or more
players). A few wild goats wander the shore
and sparse trees grow near the water. Copper
is plentiful but spread out, so you must
take control of the map; the narrow chasms
and crossings are easy to defend, but your
army may be cut off.

branches, each crossed by one shallow ford.

with matching resources and natives, who

section: control the rivers and the rich
delta for victory.

Dunas: Lençóis Maranhenses: low, flat land
covered by large sand dunes, with freshwater
lagoons between them and the largest in the
middle. Just outside the Amazon basin rain
is abundant, yet plants and animals are
scarce: the few hunts and trees, and the
more plentiful mines, will not last into the
late game, so a quick attack can decide it.

ESOC Pampas Sierras: A semi-arid zone of
highlands and chokepoints, where resources
are not scarce but spread over the whole
region. A plateau in the west is home to
many wild llamas, and in games with two

of the map. There is no trade route, but
Inca and Mapuche villages offer allies.

ESOC Thar Desert: The Thar Desert was a
waypoint for merchants on the Silk Road.
This big, dry land has little wildlife but
plenty of copper. Lost in the desert, you
never know where your settlement will be:
starting positions change every game, yet
hunts and mines are placed so that every
player gets the same.

islands on both sides of the Equator, famed
for its many endemic species. Players may
start on any island, even beside an enemy,

stand on some islands, and food on land
comes from crabs, iguanas and giant
tortoises.

Lrg Wakhan: The rugged Wakhan Corridor in
eastern Afghanistan. A deep canyon with a
single crossing separates the teams, and
each side has two or more Sufi or Udasi
villages and, with two teams, its own trade
route. Ibex, Marco Polo sheep and silver are
plentiful, and the canyon floor usually
holds extra silver and powerful treasures.

wetland deep in South America. Half of the
map lies under shallow water, so some areas
cannot be reached by land; the forests are
dense and colourful, wildlife is plentiful,
and native villages stand on the higher
ground.

Great Lakes: Fight around a large freshwater
lake ringed by a single long trade route,
whose control is crucial. Native villages
ring the lake, and resources, fish included,
are plentiful. Build too close to the shore
without controlling the water, and enemy
ships can shell your town late in the game.
Sometimes the lake is frozen over, a
different tactical challenge, and then all
the villages are Cree.

clumps of trees on the plains.

warm tropical seas, which promises war on
land and at sea. Carib villages stand in the

start, and whales in the western bay are a
valuable second source of coin.

possible alliances.

Lrg Marajo: At the mouth of the Amazon,
Marajo is the world's largest river island
and the second largest island in South
America. Expect lightning storms and heavy
rain over this almost flat island. With no
hunts, food comes from berries and the
fish-filled sea; take the water buffalo
herds early, as they are key late in the
game. The Carib villages can be useful
allies.

and the isles off the coast hide treasures.

the Zagros and Elburz ranges, with a desert
at its centre and resources scattered over
open ground with little vegetation. In team

west, bending in toward the centre;
free-for-all games get one circular route
around it.

Patagonia: A land with trade routes but no
natives: six Trading Post sites are the
prize. Stay near the coast for a steady
supply of wood. In team games a lake offers
tactical options: it sits in the centre,
with ways around both sides, or restricts
movement along the western side;
free-for-all games have no lake.

Lrg Llanos: A vast tropical grassland in
northwestern South America. Players start
near its forested edge; the centre can feel
empty, but small rises and dips make good
ambush spots. Many Republiqueta towns, more
with more players, can raise large armies.
There is always trade: one route circling
the plains or two crossing them.

across the map, and the Saskatchewan River
cuts across one corner, crossed at a ford
near each end. There are no mines: packs of

would mine. Bison and pronghorn keep food
plentiful.

Sertao: An arid backland cut by the São
Francisco River, whose level changes each
game. Flooded, only ships cross it, and
villages, plants and animals are more
plentiful; dry, its bed and canyon can be
walked, with fewer villages and resources;
in between, units ford it while ships keep
to the deep channel. Hunting is scarce, but
berry bushes grow among the trees.

treasures and plenty of other resources

Sonora: A twisting trade route winds through
this barren, desolate region, and many
cliffs and canyons create choke points.
Resources can be hard to find, though the
centre sometimes holds a rich ore deposit,
or else a native village. Look for Apache,
Maya or Navajo villages toward the edges of
the map.

number and place, and saloon outlaws can be
hired.

Alps separate the players, and a river with
its tributaries takes one of three courses
across the map. Deer, hares and chamois are
plentiful, and mines and treasures lie
between the valleys. Merchants and locals
have fled the war, so you fight on your own:
watch every chokepoint, as an enemy may
strike right behind your lines.

Asuncion: The ruined capital of Paraguay
after the bloodiest war in Latin American
history. Most natural resources lie at the
edges, and one narrow trade route zigzags
through the centre on one of two courses.
The fighting happens among the city's ruins,
where abandoned houses can be sacked for
extra food.

Lrg Atlas Mountains: The High Atlas walls
off the northern edge of the Sahara, and its
altitude gives it a climate more like Europe
than Africa: cedar groves dot the slopes,
where bighorn sheep and bears roam. Players
start on either side of a deep valley. There
is no trade route, but three merchant
settlements stand on the map.

Lrg Australia: Players arrive on the green
coast of the Great Southern Land, a huge map
of the whole continent with unique and
abundant wildlife. Trade routes and
immigrant settlements can be found by
exploring the vast Outback. Each player
brings six rabbits that breed to feed the
early colony. This may have been a mistake.

the fighting begins.

sea takes the rest.

Aegean: The turquoise waters of the Aegean
Sea are scattered with picturesque islands,
and a sea trade route winds through the
middle of them. In a two-team game one team
starts on the Greek mainland and the other
on the large island of Crete; with more
teams, players start on the smaller islands.

Africa: a spacious system of caverns, dim
and cramped, where thin corridors make

caches of provisions left by former
occupants lie in the caves.

Lrg Congo: In the deep heart of Africa, the
Congo offers riches to those bold enough to
claim its trade. The dense jungle cannot be
mapped: explored land goes dark again at
once, so you see only what your units see,
and foes may wait in the shadows. Highlands,
gorges and ponds break up the land.

Lrg Dallol: A scorching desert around a
sunken crater of salt pillars, geysers and
small pools, with the teams on opposite
sides. Short caravan routes cross two
opposite corners. Salt is the coin here,
from salt mines and salt trade sites, so the
crater and its edges are worth fighting for.

Easter Island: The Rapa Nui deforested this
small island long ago and abandoned it. The
Moai they left across the island hold a
secret: whoever controls them gains a mystic
trickle of wood. Volcano craters lie inland,
and wrecked European galleons full of gold
line the coast, one near every start.

Ecruteak: Two lands, one red and one white,
face each other across the water, joined by
shallow crossings on the flanks and through
a small central island. There three
legendary beasts and a band of blind monks
guard a bell tower: defeat them all and the
tower can be captured. The map has its own
music.

Lrg Ethiopian Highlands: The Roof of Africa,
Ethiopia's high-altitude heartland. Players
start on either side of a deep, dry valley
with a trade route through its middle.
Gelada baboons roam the hillsides, and with
no mines, coin comes from the native coffee
bushes. Two Orthodox monasteries and two
merchant settlements stand on the map.

Fjord: A long arm of the sea cuts deep into
snowy, cliff-lined land, with a team on each
side. On land the armies meet mainly beyond
the fjord's far end, while ships can strike
along its whole length. Cliffs and plateaus
break up the ground.

villages drive the economy.

Te Tai Poutini: The rainy, wild west coast
of New Zealand's South Island, covered in
rainforest. The sea to the northwest is full
of fish and treasure, while mountains along
the southwest keep the fighting on the
coast. Every player starts near a Wharenui
to ally with, and on land food comes from
elusive kiwis and kakapos and a few loose
sheep.

The rainy, wild west coast of New Zealand's South Island, covered in rainforest. The sea to the northwest is full of fish and treasure, while mountains along the southwest keep the fighting on the coast. Every player starts near a Wharenui to ally with, and on land food comes from elusive kiwis and kakapos and a few loose sheep.

Polynesian Atoll: A small coral atoll in the
middle of the vast Pacific. The central
lagoon teems with tropical reef fish, and
the ocean around has whales and treasures.
Guano deposits are the valuable source of
coin, and the Fale villages can be captured
for experience or trade.

Lrg Sahara: The vast wastes of the world's
largest desert, where rolling sand hills
stretch as far as the eye can see. Trees,
plants and animals are very scarce, so you
will have to rely on economics to build an
empire: the trade route and the African
trade sites. The open desert makes it hard
to defend yourself.

Sahel: The less harsh, semi-arid band
between the Sahara and the Sudanian savanna,
with more trees, plants and animals than the
Sahara. The desert fills one corner and
wooded savanna the opposite one. A camel
caravan route runs from corner to corner
through Timbuktu in the centre.

Lrg Savannah: Wide, open African grassland
with hills at either end, full of game, so
hunting fuels the economy. A trade route
crosses the plain on one of two sides, and
African trade sites offer extra goods. With
little cover and few obstacles, raids come
fast.

Lrg Scandinavia: A large, hilly northern
land of forests and small ponds, crossed by
a trade route through the middle. Each game
is summer, winter or Fimbulwinter: the
harsher the season, the fewer the hunts,
berries and sheep, and in Fimbulwinter even
the ponds are gone.

Tahiti: A Polynesian island of black sand
beaches: a large main island with a smaller
one to its south and a mountain near its
heart. Its tropical climate grows many
fruits and dense forests, but there are no
large animals to hunt, so berries, crabs and
farm animals feed the colonies.

Tuscany: This beautiful rolling hill country
was fought over by Italian city-states for
centuries. Two trade routes criss-cross the
middle of the map, and their trading post
sites are highly lucrative but fiercely
fought over. The edges of the map are
thickly forested.

Valley of the Kings: A sandy valley walled
by rock, with low rises and small oasis
pools, where ancient statues stand beside
the gold. With no natives or trade route,
the game is decided by who holds the gold
mines and hunts between the bases, while
lions or hyenas prowl away from the towns.

Lrg Van Diemen's Land: The remote west coast
of the island later renamed Tasmania. The
battle is for the only safe harbour on this
rugged coast, where a British convict
settlement, a good source of cheap labour,
stands on an island. Forests of tree ferns
and mountain ash cover the land, and the
whales out at sea are the only natural coin.

diagonally across the map between the teams,

chokepoints of the map.

Yellow River: The Yellow River is dry or in
flood at random. Dry, it recedes to leave
fertile islands and open ground where
animals gather to drink; flooded, it offers
extra resources and chokepoints, and ships
may sail it. Trade routes run along both
edges of the map, and local peoples can be
recruited as allies.

many treasures, and its dense forests mean
you will never run short of wood. Each
player starts near a Miskito or Maya

on your side, or build a dock on the far
shore and control both coasts.

the treasure-rich north, where mines are

trading post site, so the route is hard to
control.
